newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi opposition hardens stand against regime.
newsitem.headline: Burundi opposition hardens stand against regime.

text.p: The main Hutu-dominated opposition party said on Thursday it had no faith in Burundi's military regime, hardening its stand after the release of a senior party official.
Frodebu, ousted from power in an army coup last July, said the government of ethnic Tutsi Pierre Buyoya was completely illegitimate and had failed to bring peace to the country.

"I am unable to support a coup d'etat which is anti-democratic in principle. How can one recognise a regime which came to power by force?" leading Frodebu official Leonce Ngendakumana, speaker of the national assembly, told a news conference.
"I agreed to work with the regime in the interests of peace, but looking at the figures there is no security here even after six months," he added.
Authorities released Frodebu Secretary-General Augustin Nzogibwani on Tuesday after a week's solitary confinement.

Frodebu, which won elections in June 1993 before renegade troops killed Burundi's first Hutu president, agreed to work with the military-appointed government after the coup to start all-party negotiations.

But tensions between the government and Frodebu increased after the arrest of Nzogibwani and the opening of legal files against Ngendakumana and other Frodebu members accused of roles in massacres in Burundi in 1993.

"The security situation has improved and no one can deny it...but we must still redouble our efforts to bring peace," Buyoya was quoted by state radio as saying on Thursday after meeting army commanders.

The Tutsi-dominated army has recently gained the initiative in its war against Hutu rebels, conducting a sweep of rebel bases in the northern Kibira forest and grouping mainly-Hutu civilians into controlled settlements.
The U.N. human rights agency said in January 1,000 civilians had been killed in Burundi since December, almost all by the army.

A total of 178 soldiers held in Bujumbura's central prison revolted on Wednesday, forcing other prisoners to strike and shutting down prison operations in protest at being remanded for too long without trial.
"They are dissatisfied because they have not yet been brought to trial," prison director Laurent Naraguma told the independent production Studio Ijambo in Bujumbura.
More than 150,000 people have been killed in Burundi in massacres and the civil war between the army and Hutu rebels since October 1993 when president Melchior Ndadaye was killed.
Regional states imposed an economic and transport embargo on Burundi following the coup in an attempt so far in vain to force the government into unconditional talks with Hutu rebels.
